newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kinshasa dealers balk at Kabila's dollar rate.
newsitem.headline: Kinshasa dealers balk at Kabila's dollar rate.

text.p: Currency traders in Kinshasa balked at the foreign exchange rate recommended by new Alliance authorities, refusing on Wednesday to buy a dollar for more than 130,000 Zaires.
After a meeting with bankers on Tuesday, Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) fixed the buy price of the dollar at 145,000.
"I can't do better than 130,000 or I will lose money," said Pauline, one of the traders on "Wall Street" in the heart of Kinshasa's commercial district.
A big dealer at one of the city's top hotels offered the same rate. He said his stock of Zaires were from trading dollars at a rate of about 87,000.
"We can't sell them at more than 40 percent loss as the Alliance is asking," he said.
"There is a shortage of the right bank-notes as well," he said, declining to be quoted by name.

On Monday dealers announced a very high value for the Zaire, of 70,000 to the dollar, compared with 180,000 on the previous Friday. But this was a temporary move to appease the new authorities and bore no relation to economic realities, dealers said.
Zaire, renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo after the fall of President Mobutu Sese Seko's 32-year regime on May 17, has been a byword for monetary mayhem for two decades.
The Alliance says it is determined to restore order and will agree the rate at a weekly fix with bankers.
But acting Planning Minister Babi Mbai told Reuters on Monday he knew rates could not be imposed arbitrarily.
Different rates and bank-notes are used in different regions of Africa's third-biggest country.

Resistance to certain notes is intense. The new denominations introduced last January by Mobutu's penultimate government are called "Prostates", a cruel jibe at the ex-president's form of cancer, and are not in demand.

The 100,000 Zaire notes printed in the last few weeks by Mobutu's last military-led cabinet are also heavily discounted because shops dislike them. They are called "Outeniquas", after the name of the South African navy vessel where peace talks between Mobutu and Kabila failed earlier this month.
